title: Shared search and document permission propagation

opening.headline: When searching documents from multiple business units in one place, it's important to understand how the original document permissions are reflected in the search results.
body: Building a shared knowledge base introduces one risk: a pricing negotiation document from one business unit might appear in search results for employees of another business unit, or documents originally inaccessible in the source system might be cited in AI-generated responses. This happens because, once information is centralized, the original authorization boundaries can also be lost.

In this course, we first examine the fundamental workflow of collection and serving in public search. We then compare how document permissions are propagated through synchronization with identity providers, and at which point—during indexing, search, or just before response—permission conditions can be applied. Finally, we explore the causes of document mixing across business units and walk through the process of implementing separation of concerns.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the structure of public search and how document permissions are propagated.
The point where permissions are applied can be distinguished as indexing, during search, and just before response.
It is possible to identify points where privilege escalation could occur and assess the associated risks.

screens.title: We created a shared knowledge base and the documents got mixed up.
screens.lead: First, read a scenario that could actually occur within an organization. Consider thinking about where the problem might arise as you examine it.

visual.alt: A scene where department-specific documents converge into a single shared search, eliminating permission boundaries.
labels: Business Division A Pricing Negotiation Document

paragraphs: The organization that previously managed documents separately for each business unit established a shared knowledge base. Employees could now search scattered documents from a single location, significantly improving operational efficiency. However, one day, a search result from a B business unit employee unexpectedly displayed a pricing negotiation document from the A business unit.

A bigger problem is the AI-generated responses. In the original system, content from documents that were inaccessible was cited in the AI responses. While the search results list points to the documents, the AI responses paraphrase the document's content into sentences, making it difficult to retract once the information has been disseminated.

The cause is mostly the same. In the original system, access was controlled at the user and group levels; however, during the process of copying documents via public search, the permission information either did not accompany the documents or was not applied during the search step.
The question to be answered in this class is this: At which point in the search process should permissions be applied?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: This simply presents a summary of search results, making it seem like permissions are less important. Please remember that the summary still contains the content of the original text.

screens.outro: Let me recall my firsthand experience verifying the reflection of search permissions.

screens.title: Think about where permissions are being applied
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever verified whether search results reflect the user's permissions?
items.answer: The most certain way to verify is for two users with different permissions to ask the same question and compare the results. Many organizations operate without ever performing this verification. If such verification has never been conducted, there is no basis to believe that the results are reflected accurately.

items.prompt: When is the appropriate time to apply authorization conditions? Could it be when indexing the document, when searching to find candidates, or right before delivering the response? Where does this fit most appropriately?
items.answer: This can be applied to all three points, but the effectiveness varies. During indexing, access information is attached to the document; during search, the system searches only within permitted documents; just before responding, it rechecks the previously identified candidates. The principle is to ensure that documents without proper permissions do not enter the model's context. In this course, we will examine each reason step by step.

items.prompt: After recovering a former employee's permissions, was there any record of document access that they had previously used being retained in the search?
items.answer: Permission changes take effect immediately in the original system, but are reflected in the public search index only after synchronization occurs. This delay is precisely the magnitude of the risk. Therefore, synchronization mechanisms and their intervals become part of permission design.

screens.outro: Let's first examine the fundamental structure of public search.

screens.title: The basic architecture of public search: collection and serving
screens.lead: When you select the numbered marker in the flowchart, you can see what each step does. In the upper left is the indexing data collection flow, and below it is the question-answering serving flow.

visual.alt: The document is processed through a retrieval subsystem to generate embeddings, and the serving subsystem receives queries to perform search and generate responses, following a RAG reference architecture.

markers.label: Original upload
markers.title: The beginning of collection: upload and notification
markers.body: A data engineer uploads data from an external source to a Cloud Storage bucket. The external source could be an application, a database, or a streaming service. Once the upload is complete, Cloud Storage publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic to wake up the next processing step.

markers.label: Metadata
markers.title: Cloud Run functions create metadata.
markers.body: Pub/Sub messages trigger Cloud Run functions to execute processing tasks. The function processes the original data and creates metadata in JSONL format, storing it in a separate bucket. The place where ownership departments or access groups are attached in the document is precisely this metadata.

markers.label: Index generation
markers.title: The managed data store indexes documents.
markers.body: Another Pub/Sub message initiates processing in Gemini Enterprise's managed data store. It retrieves the original data and metadata, parses the documents efficiently for search, and splits them into chunks. Embeddings are automatically generated without additional configuration and become searchable vector indexes.

markers.label: Frontend
markers.title: The frontend receives a query
markers.body: The user sends a query through one of several frontends, such as a chatbot interface, a search page, or a mobile app. The frontend serves only the role of receiving the query and forwarding it to the unified backend. Regardless of the number of frontends, the authorization processing logic is centralized in a single location.

markers.label: Preprocessing
markers.title: Preprocessing in the unified backend: the point where filters are created
markers.body: The backend is a single endpoint used by all frontend applications and performs preprocessing before sending search requests. This preprocessing includes configuring filters to be applied to search queries. By applying conditions based on user affiliation and permissions at this stage, the same criteria are enforced regardless of which frontend is used. This is one of the most representative points where permission filters are applied.

markers.label: Search and Generation
markers.title: Gemini Enterprise searches and generates answers
markers.body: Gemini Enterprise creates an embedding for the query, retrieves relevant information from the index using semantic search, enhances the query with the retrieved information, and then generates a final response. This response flows through the backend to the frontend. Since the information used for enhancement is incorporated into the model's context, it becomes clear why authorization filtering must be applied in the earlier stage.

screens.outro: I will verify, from a synchronization perspective, how permission information is propagated all the way to the index.

screens.title: How are document permissions propagated?
screens.lead: The following is a note on authorization propagation design. When a highlighted section is selected, an explanation appears describing the significance of that section in authorization reflection.

data.text: The identity provider is Identify the user performing the search and, which serves as the basis for determining whether the user can access the result document. Google Workspace data must use Google Identity., when connecting only third-party data, an external IdP supporting OIDC or SAML 2.0 may be used. Data synchronization includes not only document data but also It also retrieves identity data such as roles, permissions, and users.. Full synchronization reflects all additions, modifications, and deletions; however, Incremental synchronization does not reflect identity data or deletions.. Full synchronization can be selected among 3-hour, 6-hour, 12-hour, 1-day, 3-day cycle.

marks.span: Identify the user performing the search and
marks.note: Gemini Enterprise verifies who the currently searching user is by using an identity provider, and then determines whether that user has access to the result documents. If the identity provider configuration is incorrect, the authorization decision itself becomes invalid.

marks.span: Google Workspace data must use Google Identity.
marks.note: The type of identity provider depends on the connected data source. For Google-owned data sources such as Google Workspace, Google Identity is required. External IdP selection is only available when connecting third-party sources.

marks.span: It also retrieves identity data such as roles, permissions, and users.
marks.note: Without retrieving permission information, you cannot determine who can view what during a search. Synchronization handles both document data and identity data.

marks.span: Incremental synchronization does not reflect identity data or deletions.
marks.note: Incremental synchronization retrieves only documents that have been added or modified after the last synchronization. Therefore, operations such as permission recovery or document deletion might not be reflected in the index using this method alone. For sources with high permission sensitivity, full synchronization is required.

The synchronization period is the maximum delay before a change in permissions is reflected in the index. The design process begins by determining how long it's acceptable for permission changes to be delayed before being reflected, and then selecting a period accordingly.

screens.outro: If permission information has been indexed, we will now compare when to apply that information.

screens.title: Three timing points for applying permissions and index separation
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the effects of applying permission conditions at indexing, searching, and just before responding. The last tab covers index separation, a stronger form of separation.

tabs.label: At indexing time
tabs.body:
When indexing documents, attach metadata such as owning business unit and access group together. At this stage, nothing is blocked. Instead, this step prepares the material that subsequent stages will apply filters to.

If the metadata at the indexing time is missing or inaccurate, all subsequent filters lose meaning. For example, documents lacking business unit information may either be visible to everyone or not visible to anyone at all.

tabs.label: At search time
tabs.body:
Filters based on user permission conditions are applied to queries, restricting searches to only authorized documents. The preprocessing step of the previously discussed unified backend is responsible for configuring this filter. Documents that are not authorized do not even reach the candidate pool and thus do not enter the model's context.

This point represents the most critical defense line. The fundamental principle is that documents without proper permissions must not enter the model's context, and during search, the filter directly enforces this principle.

tabs.label: Just before responding
tabs.body:
Filters once more remove candidates before exporting them. This serves as the final safety net. However, this stage is too late to use independently. Once candidates have been incorporated into the model's context, their content may inadvertently mix into the response.

Therefore, the final response filter complements rather than replaces the search filter. By implementing two layers of defense, a configuration error in one layer is prevented from directly resulting in a leak.

tabs.label: Index Separation
tabs.body:
If stronger separation is needed, index by business unit, effectively partitioning the data store. This approach makes it structurally impossible to misuse filters, thereby preventing data mixing altogether. It is suitable for sensitive data such as pricing negotiation documents or personnel information.

However, this comes at a cost. As stores increase, separate synchronization, management, and search operations are required for each store. Therefore, a common practice is to set separation levels according to risk, placing low-risk shared documents in a single shared store.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to an explanation identifying the cause of the mixed case in the business unit documents.

screens.title: Explanation: Case of mixed departmental documents (1) Identifying the cause
screens.lead: The instructor follows the step-by-step process of tracing the cause of document mixing. Selecting the right arrow advances to the next step. Pay attention to where the permission information disappears.

visual.alt: A trace diagram highlighting the point where three business unit documents are stored in a single data store and permission information is lost.
labels: Data store (combined documents across all business units)

steps.title: Step 1: Verify the current status.
steps.body: We indexed documents from three business units into a single data store. While convenient, this architecture does not enforce access boundaries at the store level. Since all documents are indexed in the same index, access control relies entirely on metadata attached to the documents and filters applied during search. Therefore, verifying the accuracy of these two components is the starting point for auditing.

steps.title: Step 2: Check whether group information is attached to the document.
steps.body: Select a few documents from the indexed set and verify whether ownership department and access group metadata is attached. If the information is missing or attached to only some documents, subsequent filters may not function properly. In this case, it is assumed that metadata was attached to most documents, but missing from some migrated documents.

steps.title: Step 3: Check if a permission filter is applied to the search request
steps.body: Next, we examine the preprocessing stage of the unified backend. We check whether user-specific conditions are applied as filters in the search query, or whether the same query is sent to all users. In this case, we assume that only one frontend applied a filter, while the other frontends issued queries without filters. This dispersion of filters across frontends was one of the causes.

steps.title: Step 4: Find the fact that only incremental synchronization was being used
steps.body: Finally, we verify the synchronization method. If only incremental synchronization was being used, user identity data and deletions would not be reflected. This would mean that previous permissions of employees who moved departments and deleted documents remained indexed. Combining these three factors, metadata gaps, dispersed filter positions, and overlapping synchronization methods result in documents being mixed up.

screens.outro: Having identified the cause, I'll now proceed to the second part involving separation of design and operation, and operational inspection.

screens.title: Explanation: Case of mixed business unit documents (2) Separation Design
screens.lead: This is the second part of the explanation. Follow the process of redesigning the separation structure and operational methods according to the identified root cause. Pay special attention to determining the separation level based on the associated risk.

steps.title: Step 5: Divide common documents from dedicated documents
steps.body: Common documents are stored in the shared repository, while business-unit-specific documents are stored in their respective business-unit repositories. Documents with high leakage risk, such as those involved in price negotiations, are completely separated into distinct repositories to ensure that filter errors do not result in data leaks. There is no need to split even common documents with low risk, and we should also consider the increasing management costs as the number of repositories grows.

steps.title: Step 6: The backend queries only the appropriate store and filter based on the context.
steps.body: Modify the pre-processing of the unified backend to query only the appropriate store and filter based on the user's affiliation. Since the filter logic resides in a single backend, the same criteria are applied regardless of frontend scaling. Adding an additional validation check just before response generation can prevent a configuration error on one side from immediately leading to a leak.

steps.title: Step 7: Adjust synchronization intervals according to authorization sensitivity
steps.body: Sources with high privilege sensitivity set synchronization intervals at short frequencies. The available intervals range from 3 hours to 3 days, so first determine the maximum allowable delay before privilege updates are reflected, and then adjust the interval accordingly. Deciding to increase the interval in an attempt to reduce change operations delays privilege updates further, thereby increasing risk.

steps.title: Step 8: Implement the authorization change and verification procedure into operations.
steps.body: Finally, include in the operating procedure a check to verify the results of the same query shortly after permissions have changed. The simplest approach is to run the same query using two accounts with different permissions and verify whether the results differ. While the design is completed once, the accuracy of permission implementation must be continuously verified during operations.

screens.outro: We will consolidate and summarize the conclusion of the case on a single screen.

screens.title: Permissions are applied before the search results are returned.
screens.lead: This summarizes the content reviewed so far as criteria for assessing the risk of privilege leakage.

paragraphs: Public search is structured such that it directly re-establishes the original authorization boundaries rather than consolidating documents into a single location. The most important principle here is that documents with mismatched permissions must be filtered out before entering the model's context—specifically during the retrieval stage. Approaches such as removing document names or adding disclaimers in the response are ineffective because they occur after documents have already been incorporated into the context, thus failing to enforce access control.

How accurately permissions are reflected is determined by two factors. The first is the identity provider. Since the identity provider serves as the basis for identifying the user being searched, the appropriate type must be selected based on the connected data source. The second is the synchronization method. Incremental synchronization does not reflect identity data or deletions, so for sources where permissions are critical, full synchronization is used and the interval is adjusted according to permission sensitivity.

The application points are divided into index creation metadata, search filtering, response-before-rechecking, and index separation. These are not mutually exclusive but rather combinations tailored to specific risk levels. Documents with low risk can be adequately protected using filtering alone, while documents with high leak costs require storage separation combined with both filtering and rechecking.

Finally, operations. To ensure the design remains sustainable, operational procedures should include a check to verify results immediately after changing permissions. Simply performing a periodic check that compares results between two users with different permissions can reveal many leaks. When assessing leakage risks, sequentially ask whether metadata is accurate, whether filters are centralized, and whether synchronization follows permission changes.

In summary, when designing shared search functionality, the following order should not be overlooked: first, design metadata to attach ownership and access information to documents; next, select an identity provider and synchronization method based on the sensitivity level of the source; then, consolidate filters for search execution into a single point; finally, distribute high-risk data across separate stores. Following this order makes it easier to trace when permissions have been lost. Whenever a new business unit or data source is added, consistently applying this same order allows expanding the shared search scope while maintaining clear permission boundaries.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Permissions should be applied before the model context is populated, and ideally before search results are returned. The accuracy is determined by the identity provider and synchronization method.

glossary.def: This is a structure that consolidates documentation from multiple sources into a single search experience.
This is the process by which the original system's user and group access permissions are reflected in the indexing and search results.
It indicates at which stage—during indexing, searching, or just before responding—the permissions are applied.
This approach separates data stores by business unit to prevent documents from being mixed.
This is a synchronization that retrieves only documents added or modified after the last sync, without reflecting identity data or deletions.

misconceptions.myth: The search results are only summaries, so permissions are less important.
misconceptions.fact: Summaries and responses also contain the original text's content. Citing a document without authorization constitutes a leak similar to revealing the original text.

misconceptions.myth: When a document is indexed, the original's permissions are automatically inherited.
misconceptions.fact: Entity provider configuration and synchronization, along with search filter design, are required for permissions to be reflected.
Incremental synchronization does not reflect identity data or deletions, which may result in delayed updates for permission revocation and document deletion.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Apply permissions before the model context is loaded, ideally before search results are returned.
The authentication provider and synchronization method determine the accuracy of permission reflection.
Combines indexing metadata, search filters, and index separation according to risk levels.
Integrate a review to verify results after permission changes into operations.
